# Why Visualize? {background-color="#28A87D"}

## Statistics Hide What Pictures Reveal {.smaller}

- **Anscombe's Quartet** — four datasets, identical mean / sd / correlation, four completely different shapes
- **Datasaurus Dozen** — thirteen datasets with the same summary stats; one of them is literally a dinosaur
- Means and standard deviations do not see structure, outliers, batch effects, or non-linear trends
- A scatter plot of the raw points exposes all of them in a second
- Publication-quality visualization is part of the scientific argument, not an afterthought
- This is why we visualize *before* we model


## Big Data in Biology {.smaller}

- Human genome: 3 × 10⁹ bp · 20 000 genes · 4 M common SNPs
- A single scRNA-seq experiment: 10⁵ cells × 2 × 10⁴ genes
- 1000 Genomes Project: 2 504 individuals · 88 M variants
- Modern GWAS: 10⁶ – 10⁷ variants × 10⁵ – 10⁶ individuals
- ChIP-seq / ATAC-seq peaks: 10⁵ regions across the genome per experiment
- No human can read these as numbers — visualization is the only way to understand them


## The Python Visualization Ecosystem {.smaller}

- **matplotlib** — the foundation everything else builds on (imperative, full control)
- **seaborn** — high-level statistical wrappers around matplotlib
- **plotly** — interactive web-native figures
- **scanpy / squidpy** — single-cell and spatial omics
- **pyCirclize / pyMSAviz / toytree** — domain-specific genomics views
- **genomics_course** *(this course)* — one-line, style-locked publication figures


# From ggplot2 to Python {background-color="#28A87D"}

## ggplot2 → Python Mental Map {.smaller}

| ggplot2 (R) | Python equivalent |
|-------------|-------------------|
| `aes(color = group)` | color kwarg / palette dict |
| `geom_point()` | `ax.scatter()` |
| `geom_line()` | `ax.plot()` |
| `facet_wrap(~group)` | `fig, axes = plt.subplots()` |
| `theme()` | `rcParams` + `ax.set_*()` |
| `scale_color_manual()` | palette dict |
| `labs(title = ..., x = ..., y = ...)` | `ax.set_title / xlabel / ylabel` |
| `ggsave()` | `fig.savefig(..., dpi = 300)` |

> The grammar is the same — only the syntax changes. In this course every plot is a one-line call into `genomics_course.plots`, so you do not write matplotlib by hand.


# Volcano Plots {background-color="#28A87D"}

## Volcano Plot — What & Why

- A scatter of **effect size vs statistical significance** for differential expression
- **x-axis**: log₂ fold change — direction and magnitude of regulation
- **y-axis**: −log₁₀(p-value) — significance
- Genes in the **upper corners** are both strongly regulated and highly significant
- Standard summary figure for RNA-seq, scRNA-seq pseudo-bulk, and proteomics


## Volcano Plot — Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[DESeq2 results table] --> B[Compute &minus;log&#8321;&#8320; padj]
    B --> C[Classify NS / FC / p / both]
    C --> D[Scatter coloured by class]
    D --> E[Label top-N genes]
    E --> F[Add LFC and p threshold lines]
```


## Volcano Plot — Result {.plot-slide}

```{python}
fig = plot_volcano(load_deseq2())
save(fig, "figures/volcano.png")
```

# Manhattan Plots {background-color="#28A87D"}

## Manhattan Plot — What & Why

- The canonical summary figure for **GWAS** (genome-wide association studies)
- **x-axis**: genomic position, chromosomes laid end to end
- **y-axis**: −log₁₀(p-value) of association with the phenotype
- **Peaks above the dashed line** mark loci that pass genome-wide significance (5 × 10⁻⁸)
- Alternating chromosome colours let the eye follow position at a glance


## Manhattan Plot — Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[GWAS summary stats] --> B[Sort by chrom and bp]
    B --> C[Cumulative x position]
    C --> D[Compute &minus;log&#8321;&#8320; p]
    D --> E[Alternate colours per chrom]
    E --> F[Add genome-wide significance line]
```


## Manhattan Plot — Result {.plot-slide}

```{python}
fig = plot_manhattan(load_gwas())
save(fig, "figures/manhattan.png")
```

# Admixture Plots {background-color="#28A87D"}

## Admixture Plot — What & Why

- Visualises **ancestry proportions** estimated by ADMIXTURE / STRUCTURE / fastSTRUCTURE
- Each vertical bar = one individual, segments = inferred ancestry across **K** components
- Populations separated by thin white lines; individuals sorted within each population
- Used in human population genetics, conservation, crops, hybrid-zone analysis
- The dominant ancestry per population is read from the bar colour pattern


## Admixture Plot — Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Genotype matrix] --> B[ADMIXTURE / STRUCTURE]
    B --> C[Q-matrix: ancestry per individual]
    C --> D[Sort individuals within population]
    D --> E[Stacked bars, width = 1]
    E --> F[White separators between populations]
```


## Admixture Plot — Result {.plot-slide}

```{python}
fig = plot_admixture(load_admixture(K=5))
save(fig, "figures/admixture_K5.png")
```

# Variant Effect / LLD {background-color="#28A87D"}

## LLD Plot — What & Why

- **L**og-**L**ikelihood **D**ifference (or any diverging variant-level score)
- Horizontal bar chart sorted by magnitude, coloured by semantic class
- Standard layout: pathogenic on one side of the zero line, benign on the other
- Gene labels read cleanly because they sit on the y-axis
- Classification sub-labels (*pathogenic*, *risk*, *benign*) below each gene name


## LLD Plot — Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Variant table] --> B[Sort by LLD]
    B --> C[Assign semantic colour]
    C --> D[Horizontal bars]
    D --> E[Values at bar ends]
    E --> F[Zero reference line]
```


## LLD Plot — Result {.plot-slide}

```{python}
fig = plot_lld(load_variants())
save(fig, "figures/lld.png")
```

# Topics Reserved for Next Release {background-color="#28A87D"}

The following methods will be released in the next `genomics_course` versions. Each follows the same pattern — `from genomics_course.plots import plot_*` and a single function call.


## Dimensionality Reduction — What & Why {.smaller}

- **PCA**, **t-SNE**, **UMAP** — three ways to project thousands of genes onto 2D
- PCA: linear, fast, exact variance accounting; quick QC of batch effects
- t-SNE: non-linear, preserves local neighbourhoods, slow on > 50 k cells
- UMAP: non-linear, preserves more global structure, scales to single-cell atlases
- Standard scRNA-seq workflow: PCA (50 PCs) → UMAP for visualisation
- Reserved API: `plot_pca`, `plot_tsne`, `plot_umap`


## Dimensionality Reduction — Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Cells x Genes matrix] --> B[Normalise + log]
    B --> C[Select highly variable genes]
    C --> D[Scale + PCA to 50D]
    D --> E[k-NN graph]
    E --> F[UMAP / t-SNE to 2D]
    F --> G[Colour by cell type]
```


## Heatmaps — What & Why {.smaller}

- **Two-way visualisation** — rows are genes, columns are samples (or vice versa)
- Cells are coloured by expression z-score on a diverging blue–white–red palette
- Clustering of rows / columns reveals co-expression modules and sample groups
- The bread-and-butter figure of any RNA-seq study
- Used for gene signatures, marker panels, time-course experiments
- Reserved API: `plot_heatmap` (with side-annotation tracks)


## Heatmaps — Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Expression matrix] --> B[Filter low-count genes]
    B --> C[Z-score per gene]
    C --> D[Hierarchical clustering]
    D --> E[Diverging blue-white-red colourmap]
    E --> F[Side annotation tracks]
```


## Waffle & Waterfall — What & Why {.smaller}

- **Waffle** — proportion of a cohort by category as a square grid of icons
- **Waterfall** — patients sorted left-to-right by mutation burden (TMB)
- Used in clinical genomics, oncology cohorts, immune repertoire analysis
- Waterfall layout is preferred over barplots for TMB because the ranking carries meaning
- Star markers above bars flag MSI-H or other clinically relevant subsets
- Reserved API: `plot_waffle`, `plot_waterfall`


## Waffle & Waterfall — Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Cohort table] --> B{Plot type?}
    B -- proportion --> C[Counts to 10x10 grid]
    C --> D[Icons coloured by category]
    B -- TMB ranking --> E[Sort patients by SNV count]
    E --> F[Coloured bars + MSI star markers]
```


## Peak Visualization — What & Why {.smaller}

- ChIP-seq / ATAC-seq / CUT&RUN — stacked signal tracks across a genomic locus
- Each row = one experiment; x-axis = genomic position
- Gene annotation track at the bottom shows exons and strand
- Shared peaks across tracks are highlighted with a vertical shaded band
- Standard view for inspecting regulatory regions and enhancers
- Reserved API: `plot_peaks` (multi-track with gene annotation)


## Peak Visualization — Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[BigWig / BED files] --> B[Slice region of interest]
    B --> C[Per-track filled area]
    C --> D[Gene annotation track]
    D --> E[Strand arrows]
    E --> F[Shared peak highlight]
```


## Pathway & Annotation Plots — What & Why {.smaller}

- After differential expression you ask: *which pathways are enriched?*
- Standard outputs: horizontal bar chart of top GO / KEGG / Reactome terms
- Bubble plot: gene-ratio on x-axis, dot size = gene count, colour = significance
- Used for any over-representation or GSEA result
- Direction-aware comparison: up- vs down-regulated gene sets side by side
- Reserved API: `plot_enrichment_bar`, `plot_enrichment_bubble`


## Pathway & Annotation Plots — Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Significant gene list] --> B[Enrichment vs background]
    B --> C[Adjusted p-values]
    C --> D[Top-N pathways]
    D --> E[Horizontal bars or bubble]
    E --> F[Threshold line at padj = 0.05]
```
